title: Walking past a stranger
note:
Cover for an activity not built yet; the worklist alt text is the brief. Uses the outdoor block for the pavement and the foliage band.

Two things have to be true at once and they pull against each other: Lucy is WALKING, and the leash is SLACK. A walking dog is easy to draw taut, and rounds 1-19 of the tan era record exactly that failure — the leash pulled straight, which reads as pulling. So the deep J of slack is named explicitly, as is her shoulder being level with the handler's knee, which is what stopped her reading as out in front.

The stranger must be a stranger: passing behind, not interacting, not looking, not stopping. He is deliberately NOT the guest — no blue hoodie, no black cap — because the guest is a specific character who visits the house, and reusing him here would make this look like a greeting.

Round 54 got the leash, the stranger and the palette right and put Lucy behind the handler: her shoulder sat at x480 against a knee at x700, so her whole body trailed the handler's legs. That is the defect docs/pilot-prompts.md records for the tan-era walking picture — 'she currently trails behind the handler' — and the fix there was the same, to move the dog forward. 'Shoulder level with the knee' was read as a height rather than a position, so it now says a vertical line through the knee with her shoulder on it.

The plumb-line clause was relaxed after three rounds. Round 54 put Lucy's shoulder at x480 against a knee at x700, round 55 moved it to x530, and round 56 — told the plumb line should land on her shoulder blade — overshot her whole body past the handler's leading foot, which is the defect docs/pilot-prompts.md records as 'reads as pulling' and is worse than trailing, because pulling is the behaviour this activity teaches against. Round 55 ships: beside the handler, clear daylight between them, muzzle up, leash clipped and deeply slack. The claim now asks for what that picture guarantees — beside and not ahead — rather than an exact alignment three attempts could not hit. Same call as door-stay-cover: a review question the picture fails is a false pass on every future round.
scene: Outdoors on a plain grey pavement with flat lawn beside it and the flat spruce foliage band behind — no building, no porch, no door, no fence and no road anywhere in the picture. The handler WALKS from left to right in profile, upright and easy. Lucy walks at her side on the near hand, in profile, moving with her: SHE WALKS ALONGSIDE THE HANDLER, NOT BEHIND HER, and this is about her position across the picture rather than her height: if you dropped a PLUMB LINE straight down from the handler's near knee it would land on Lucy's SHOULDER BLADE — not on her hip, not on her tail, not on the ground behind her. That means her head and neck reach FORWARD PAST the handler's near leg and her chest is roughly beneath the handler's hip, which is what a dog walking at heel actually looks like. She is that far forward. Her body must NOT trail back behind the handler's legs — a dog whose whole body sits behind the handler reads as lagging or being towed, which is a different picture. At the same time her nose must not go further forward than the handler's leading foot: she is level with her, never out in front. Leave clear daylight between Lucy's body and the handler's near leg so her whole silhouette and the leash stay readable — she is beside her, not overlapping her. Lucy's head is up and her whole muzzle is tipped up toward the handler's face; her ears are up, her tail level, her gait relaxed. THE LEASH IS ATTACHED AND SLACK: its clip is closed on the D-ring at the front of her collar, and the line runs from that ring up to the handler's near hand held low, hanging in a deep obvious J of slack along the way — it is never straight and never taut, because a taut line reads as pulling. Follow it with your eye from collar to hand without a break. BEHIND THEM, a stranger walks the other way in the background, small and well back — an ordinary adult in muted neutral clothes, NOT in a blue hoodie and NOT in a black cap, because that is the household's guest and this is not him. He is not looking at Lucy, not stopping, not reaching, not interacting: he is simply passing. Neither Lucy nor the handler is looking at him. HOW BIG THEY ARE DRAWN: draw the figures SMALLER than the composition wants, grouped close together near the middle rather than spread across the frame. The top of the highest head sits about a QUARTER of the way down from the top edge and no higher; the lowest thing that matters no lower than three quarters of the way down. Above every head leave a clear band of empty background at least a fifth of the picture height with nothing in it, and below them clear empty ground. Left and right, nothing that matters enters the outer eighth of the width. The app crops this two ways at once — a wide Today band keeping only the middle strip of the HEIGHT, and a centred square keeping only the middle three-quarters of the WIDTH — so a head near the top edge is decapitated on the app largest surface. Empty background above them is better than a sliced head.
mustBeTrue: the leash is visibly clipped to the D-ring at the front of Lucy's collar and hangs in a deep J of slack all the way to the handler's low hand, never straight or taut; Lucy walks beside the handler and not ahead of her — her nose no further forward than the handler's leading foot — with clear daylight between her body and the handler's near leg, and her muzzle tipped up toward the handler's face; the stranger is small, well behind them, in muted neutral clothes rather than a blue hoodie or black cap, and is passing without looking at or interacting with either of them; and the top of the handler's head sits about a quarter of the way down the frame with clear background above it and nothing that matters in the top fifth, the bottom quarter or the outer eighth of either side.
